strengths: The theory of the paper, to be best of my understanding, is sound and accurate. The statement of the theorems, lemmas, and the proofs, as much as I delved into, are sound and clearly stated.
The main problem that this paper focuses on, is a natural abstraction of real-world problems.
There are many clever and intuitive proof techniques used in this work, which may be interesting for the reader
The problem is very relevant, as many works which utilize permutation invariant functions do not consider the importance of the embedding dimension.
The derivation in the text appears thorough and rigorous

The paper presents novel ideas in designing the feature map \(\Phi : \mathbb{R}^{N \times D} \to \mathbb{R}^L\) to overcome limitations of previous work which did not generalize beyond the scalar-elements case (i.e., D=1).
The combinatorial argument presented in the proof of Lemma 4.4 is particularly nice, though it is somewhat difficult to follow in the current exposition.
Overall, I find the proofs insightful and quite surprising (I will elaborate on this below). Hence, I am inclined to accepting this paper.

The contrast to the Zweig and Bruna lower bound is of theoretical interest, since it shows that requiring analytic activation functions changes the minimum width cost from polynomial in N and D to exponential.

The work, coupled with its experimental results, suggests that an impressive amount of information can be encoded in sums of relatively low-dimensional feature embeddings, and that the functions that cannot be represented by standard DeepSets architectures are likely highly pathological or discontinuous.
The results are technically impressive, and I found no major errors in the proofs.
In particular, the LP and LE constructions were clever, meticulous, and well-visualized by figures.
weaknesses: While the paper presents a mathematically intriguing case, I am not quite sure what to draw from it from a machine learning perspective. The theoretical result is not tied to any practical algorithm, limiting its impact on the field.

Despite the embedding-sum decomposition, the construction of the \(\rho\) function \(\rho:R^L \to R\) is still a complete black box; the paper proves the existence of such a function, but does not provide any details on its structure, complexity, or how it can be implemented, making it difficult to translate the theoretical results into practical applications.

The paper could benefit from more high-level idea developments both before and after the theorems; a lack of geometric intuition makes the proofs harder to grasp and limits the broader understanding of the core ideas.

The notion of injectivity for functions (Def 2.7), that \(f(X) = f(X')\) implies rows of \(X\) are a permutation of rows of \(X'\), slightly deviates from the standard notion and could lead to confusion for readers.
The notation \([a\ x]\sim [a'\ x']\) is somewhat ambiguous; it would be helpful to highlight that this implies stacking the vectors rather than concatenation.
"Comparison with Prior Arts"? This informal phrasing seems inappropriate; authors likely mean "articles".
(page 17) "pigeon-hold principle" appears to be a typo for "pigeonhole principle".
It took me a while to grasp the concept of anchors. In Lemma 4.2 the same anchor is being applied over all the channels, but this should be stressed in plain text as well.

The sentence in Lemma 4.2 that says "once each coupled pairs are aligned, two data matrices are globally aligned" is unclear; the notion of "aligned" and "globally aligned" needs a more rigorous definition in the context of set functions and permutation invariance.

The necessity of Lemma 4.4 is not well explained; it is unclear how the construction involving mixing anchor channels with original feature channels is crucial for the proof and how it motivates the alignment of the original data matrices.
The exposition is quite hard to follow; the paper would benefit from less confusing notation and a more structured and detailed proof overview.

All linear projections that form the coordinates of \(\phi(x^i)\) are represented as \(w_j\)’s; using different symbols for the different types of these mappings (standard basis, anchors, \(\gamma\)s, etc.) would be more informative.

In p.7, the superscript notation for \(w\) is confusing because it is used both to index elements of the set and to denote different types of \(w\); using distinct symbols would avoid unnecessary superscripts.
The non‑explicitness of the construction means that \(\rho\) is likely to be a highly non‑smooth function that is difficult to compactly approximate using a neural network architecture.

I was momentarily confused by the conditions on \(L\) in Theorem 3.1; it is unclear whether the bound is an upper bound on the smallest \(L\) or a restriction that \(L\) cannot exceed a certain value, so the lower bounds could be mentioned separately for clarity.

Lemma E.1 is much easier to parse after noting Remark E.2; the remark could be included before the proof, or the lemma could define the \(\gamma_i\) values explicitly as prime numbers, since the generality is not needed for the proofs.
